/java/core-java/oop-and-design.The pillars, with the senior-level angle: The four pillars are four habits: hide the details (encapsulation), show only the useful part (abstraction), reuse by extending (inheritance), and treat different objects the same way when they share an interface (polymorphism). In the table below, read the "Textbook" column first; the last column is extra depth you can skip for now.
/java/core-java/oop-and-design.Interface or abstract class?: An interface says *what* a class can do and stores no data. An abstract class is a half-finished class: it can hold data and shared code, but you cannot create it directly. A class can implement many interfaces but extend only one class. When unsure, start with an interface.

/java/core-java/collections-framework.Hierarchy at a glance: Everything starts from `Collection` (lists, sets, queues). `Map` is separate because it holds key-value pairs, not single items. Sets are built on top of maps internally.
/java/core-java/collections-framework.Complexity cheat sheet: "O(1)" means the time does not grow with the amount of data; "O(n)" means it grows in step with it; "O(log n)" grows slowly. For a beginner: lists are good for reading by position, `HashMap` is great for finding by key, and searching a list item by item gets slow for big lists.
/java/core-java/collections-framework.Lists: `ArrayList` is a resizable array and should be your default list. `LinkedList` is rarely the better choice. `List.of(...)` makes a list that cannot be changed.
/java/core-java/collections-framework.Maps and sets: Use `HashMap` to find values by key quickly, `HashSet` to keep unique values, `LinkedHashMap` to remember insertion order, and `TreeMap` when keys must stay sorted.
/java/core-java/collections-framework.Choosing, quickly: Quick rule: a list means `ArrayList`; a stack or queue means `ArrayDeque`; lookup by key means `HashMap`; unique items means `HashSet`; sorted means `TreeMap` or `TreeSet`.

/java/core-java/equals-hashcode.The equals contract: `equals` must behave like a sensible "same as" test: an object equals itself, if a equals b then b equals a, and the answer does not randomly change. Comparing with `null` must give false. The page shows a correct implementation you can copy.
/java/core-java/equals-hashcode.Implementation guidance: Practical rules: compare the same fields in `equals` and `hashCode`, use `Objects.equals` for fields that may be null, and use a record when you just need a data holder, because records generate both methods for you.

/java/core-java/exceptions.The hierarchy: Every problem is a `Throwable`. `Error` means the JVM is in trouble (for example out of memory) and you should not catch it. `Exception` splits into checked ones (like `IOException`) and `RuntimeException` ones (like `NullPointerException`).
/java/core-java/exceptions.Checked or unchecked?: A simple rule: if the caller can reasonably recover (retry, ask the user), a checked exception is fine; for programming mistakes use unchecked ones. Modern code uses unchecked exceptions most of the time.
/java/core-java/exceptions.try-with-resources: Put things that must be closed (files, connections) in the `try (...)` parentheses and Java closes them for you, even when an error happens. This replaces the old habit of closing them in `finally`.
/java/core-java/exceptions.finally traps: `finally` always runs, which is great for cleanup. But never `return` or throw from inside `finally`: it can silently hide the real error.

/java/core-java/streams-and-lambdas.Stream pipelines are lazy: Think of a stream as an assembly line. `filter` and `map` only describe the steps; nothing moves until you call a final operation such as `toList()` or `count()`. A stream can be used only once.
/java/core-java/streams-and-lambdas.Collectors worth knowing: Collectors turn a stream back into a result: `groupingBy` makes groups (like SQL GROUP BY), `toMap` builds a map, `joining` glues strings together. `toMap` throws an error if two items have the same key unless you give it a merge rule.
/java/core-java/streams-and-lambdas.Optional: guidelines: `Optional` is a box that may be empty, used as a return value instead of returning `null`. Prefer `orElse`, `map` and `orElseThrow` over calling `get()` directly.

/java/core-java/modern-java.Timeline (LTS in bold): Read this table as a map. You do not need to memorise every version; remember the LTS versions and the headline feature of each.
/java/core-java/modern-java.Language features worth adopting: Learn these first: `var`, switch expressions, text blocks, records (small immutable data classes), and sealed classes with pattern matching.

/java/core-java/hashmap-internals.Structure: Picture an array of drawers. The key's hash number decides which drawer it goes into. If two keys land in the same drawer, they are chained together. The default is 16 drawers, and the map grows when it is about 75% full.
/java/core-java/hashmap-internals.Keys: the contract that makes it work: Keys must give a stable hash code and a correct `equals`. If you change a key object after putting it in the map, the map looks in the wrong drawer and can no longer find it. Use immutable keys such as `String`, numbers or records.

/java/core-java/generics.Raw types: A raw type is a generic class used without its type, such as `List` instead of `List<String>`. It switches off compiler checks and can cause a `ClassCastException` later. Avoid it in new code.

/java/core-java/immutability.Why it matters: Because an immutable object cannot change, you can share it freely, use it as a map key, and never worry about another thread modifying it. The cost is creating a new object for every change.
/java/core-java/immutability.Recipe for an immutable class: Five steps: make the class `final`, make fields `private final`, add no setters, copy mutable things such as lists when they come in and go out, and do not let `this` escape from the constructor.
/java/core-java/immutability.String immutability: Strings cannot change, so Java can safely share one copy of a literal (the string pool) and cache its hash code. Use `StringBuilder` when building text in a loop.

/java/concurrency-jvm/threads-basics.What a thread is: Think of a thread as a worker in a kitchen. Several workers (threads) share the same ingredients (memory). Each worker has a private notepad (the stack) for what they are doing right now.
/java/concurrency-jvm/threads-basics.Thread states: A thread moves between a few states: new, runnable (ready or running), blocked or waiting (paused), and terminated. You will see these names in thread dumps.
/java/concurrency-jvm/threads-basics.Creating threads: Write the task as a `Runnable` or a lambda, then give it to a thread or, better, an executor. Always call `start()`; calling `run()` just executes the code on the current thread.
/java/concurrency-jvm/threads-basics.Daemon threads: A daemon thread is a background helper. When only daemon threads are left, the JVM exits. Never use daemon threads for work that must finish.

/java/concurrency-jvm/synchronization-an.synchronized: Put `synchronized` on a method or block, and Java lets only one thread in at a time for that object. It also makes the changes visible to the next thread that enters. Keep synchronized blocks short.

/java/concurrency-jvm/garbage-collection.Generational hypothesis: Most objects live very briefly, such as temporary values inside a request. So Java cleans the young area often (fast) and the old area rarely (slow). This is why creating many short-lived objects is usually fine.

/spring/core/ioc-and-dependency-injectio.Container basics: The container creates your objects (beans) at startup and wires them together. `ApplicationContext` is what you actually use. If the wiring is wrong, the application fails at startup, which is a good thing.
/spring/core/ioc-and-dependency-injectio.Defining beans: Two ways: annotate your own class with `@Component` (or `@Service`, `@Repository`, `@Controller`) and Spring finds it, or write a `@Bean` method for classes you do not own.
/spring/core/ioc-and-dependency-injectio.Injection styles: Prefer constructor injection: list the dependencies as constructor parameters. It makes them required, lets fields be `final`, and makes the class easy to unit test without Spring.

/spring/core/bean-lifecycle-and-scopes.Scopes: Scope decides how many objects Spring makes. `singleton` (default): one for the whole app. `prototype`: a new one each time you ask. `request` and `session` exist in web apps: one per HTTP request or per user session.

/spring/core/aop-and-proxies.Vocabulary: Four words to know: an *aspect* is the extra behaviour, *advice* is the code that runs, a *pointcut* says which methods it applies to, and a *join point* is the moment it runs (a method call, in Spring).

/spring/core/configuration-profiles-cond.@Configuration and @Bean: A `@Configuration` class is a place to define beans by hand. Each `@Bean` method returns an object that Spring then manages. Pass dependencies in as method parameters.
/spring/core/configuration-profiles-cond.Component scanning: Spring searches your packages for classes annotated with `@Component` and its variants and registers them as beans. Put the main class in the root package so everything below it is found.
/spring/core/configuration-profiles-cond.Profiles: A profile is a named group of settings such as `dev` or `prod`. Activate one with `spring.profiles.active`, and beans or property files marked for that profile are used.

/spring/core/application-events.Publishing and listening: Publisher: `events.publishEvent(new OrderPlaced(id))`. Listener: a method annotated `@EventListener` that takes the event as a parameter. The publisher does not know who is listening.

/spring/boot/overview.What Boot gives you: Boot removes setup work: starters choose compatible library versions, auto-configuration builds common beans, an embedded Tomcat means no separate server to install, and Actuator shows health and metrics.
/spring/boot/overview.What happens at startup: `SpringApplication.run` loads your settings, creates the application context, creates all beans, starts the web server, and then runs any startup runners. If something is mis-wired, it fails here.

/spring/boot/starters.Two separate ideas: Starters decide *which libraries* you get. Dependency management decides *which versions* of them. Together, you add one dependency and everything is compatible.
/spring/boot/starters.Getting the BOM: The BOM (bill of materials) is the list of tested versions. You get it either by using `spring-boot-starter-parent` as your Maven parent, or by importing `spring-boot-dependencies`.
/spring/boot/starters.Frequently used starters: The ones you will use most: web (REST APIs), data-jpa (database access), validation, security, actuator (monitoring) and test.

/spring/boot/configuration.Precedence (highest wins), simplified: If the same setting appears in several places, the more specific one wins: command-line arguments beat environment variables, which beat profile files, which beat `application.yml`. That is how production overrides development.
/spring/boot/configuration.Profiles: Create `application-dev.yml` and `application-prod.yml` and activate one with `spring.profiles.active`. Only the active profile's file is applied on top of the default file.
/spring/boot/configuration.@Value versus @ConfigurationProperties: `@Value` reads one setting. `@ConfigurationProperties` binds a whole group of settings (a prefix such as `payment`) to a typed class and can validate it. Use the second for anything beyond one or two values.

/spring/boot/exception-handling.The layers: There are several ways to handle errors, from Boot's default error response up to a global `@RestControllerAdvice`. The global advice is the one to use in real projects.
/spring/boot/exception-handling.Example: The example has a custom exception, a handler that turns it into a 404 response, and a catch-all handler that hides unexpected errors behind a generic 500 message.

/spring/boot/validation.Validating a request body: Annotate the fields of your request class (`@NotNull`, `@Size`, `@Email`) and write `@Valid @RequestBody` in the controller. Nested objects need `@Valid` too, otherwise they are not checked.
/spring/boot/validation.Validating path variables and request pa: For values in the URL, put `@Validated` on the controller class and constraints directly on the parameters, such as `@PathVariable @Min(1) long id`.
/spring/boot/validation.Returning field errors: When validation fails, Spring throws an exception. A small handler turns it into a 400 response listing each bad field and its message.

/spring/boot/testing-basics.A unit test without Spring: Because the service takes its dependencies in the constructor, you can test it with `new` and Mockito mocks. No Spring context is needed, so the test runs in milliseconds.
/spring/boot/testing-basics.Mockito cheatsheet: The three things you will use most: `when(x.foo()).thenReturn(y)` to set up a fake answer, `verify(x).foo()` to check a call happened, and `assertThatThrownBy` (AssertJ) to check an exception.

/spring/boot/auto-configuration.Seeing what Boot decided: Run with `--debug` (or open `/actuator/conditions`) and Boot prints which auto-configurations were applied (positive matches) and which were skipped and why (negative matches).
/spring/boot/auto-configuration.Overriding and excluding: To replace something Boot creates, define your own bean of that type. To switch an auto-configuration off completely, use `exclude` on `@SpringBootApplication`.

/spring/boot/actuator.Exposure is opt-in: By default only `health` is visible over HTTP. You list other endpoints in `management.endpoints.web.exposure.include`, and you should expose as few as possible because some reveal sensitive data.

/spring/boot/testing-slices-testcontaine.Slice annotations: A slice annotation loads only what that layer needs. `@WebMvcTest` loads controllers and JSON handling but not services; `@DataJpaTest` loads repositories and Hibernate but not controllers.

/spring/data/jpa-basics.A small domain: The example uses orders and order items. An order has many items (`@OneToMany`) and each item points back to its order (`@ManyToOne`). Mark associations `LAZY` so data is loaded only when needed.
/spring/data/jpa-basics.The persistence context: Inside a transaction Hibernate keeps track of the entities it loaded. If you change one, it notices and writes the update when the transaction commits, so you often do not need to call `save`.
/spring/data/jpa-basics.Repositories: Extend `JpaRepository<Entity, IdType>` and Spring writes the implementation. Method names such as `findByStatus` become queries automatically.

/spring/data/n-plus-one-lazy-loading.What it is: Example: loading 100 orders and then reading each order's items causes 1 + 100 = 101 database calls. The fix is to ask for the items in the same query.

/spring/data/transactions.How @Transactional works: Spring wraps your service in a proxy. The proxy begins a transaction, calls your method, and commits or rolls back. Because it is a proxy, a method calling another method in the same class bypasses it.

/spring/data/sql-tuning-indexing.How an index works: Most indexes are B-trees: a sorted structure the database can search quickly. Searching 10 million rows through an index takes a handful of steps instead of 10 million.
/spring/data/sql-tuning-indexing.Declaring indexes: You can declare indexes in JPA annotations, but in real projects you create them in migration scripts (Flyway or Liquibase) so every environment gets the same schema.

/spring/data/caching.Layers of caching in a Spring applicatio: Caching exists at several layers: browser and CDN, your application (`@Cacheable`), Hibernate, and the database itself. Start with application caching for slow, repeated reads.
/spring/data/caching.Spring Cache abstraction: `@Cacheable` stores a method's result, `@CachePut` always runs and refreshes it, and `@CacheEvict` removes it. They use the same proxy mechanism as `@Transactional`.

/spring/security/security-architecture.Core concepts: Authentication means proving who you are. Authorisation means checking what you may do. The result of authentication is stored in the `SecurityContext` for the current request.
/spring/security/security-architecture.Roles vs authorities: An authority is a permission string such as `orders.read`. A role is an authority that starts with `ROLE_`. `hasRole('ADMIN')` checks for the authority `ROLE_ADMIN`.
/spring/security/security-architecture.Passwords: Never store plain passwords. Spring's `PasswordEncoder` (bcrypt by default) stores a salted, slow hash, so stolen hashes are hard to crack.

/spring/security/jwt.Structure: A JWT has three parts separated by dots: a header (the algorithm), a payload (claims such as `sub` and `exp`), and a signature. The payload is only encoded, not encrypted.

/spring/security/common-vulnerabilities.1. *: IDOR means changing an id in the URL to see someone else's data. The fix is to check on the server that the logged-in user owns the object, every time.
/spring/security/common-vulnerabilities.2. *: Injection happens when user input is glued into a query. Use parameters (`?` or `:name`) so the input is always treated as data, never as SQL.
/spring/security/common-vulnerabilities.3. *: XSS lets an attacker run script in other users' browsers. Escape output (most templates do it by default) and set a Content-Security-Policy.

/microservices/overview.Monolith versus microservices: A monolith is one deployable application. Microservices are many small ones. Microservices help large teams move independently, but add network calls, many deployments and harder debugging.

/microservices/infrastructure/api-gatewa.Typical responsibilities: A gateway usually handles routing by URL, checking tokens, limiting requests, and adding headers such as a correlation id. Business rules stay in the services.

/microservices/infrastructure/service-di.The three steps: 1. Register: a service tells the registry its name and address. 2. Heartbeat: it keeps saying it is alive. 3. Lookup: callers ask the registry for healthy instances by name.

/microservices/communication/service-com.REST with RestClient: `RestClient` is Spring's modern way to call another service over HTTP: `client.get().uri(...).retrieve().body(MyType.class)`. Always set connect and read timeouts.

/microservices/resilience/resilience4j.The patterns: Each pattern solves a different problem: timeout (do not wait forever), retry (try again), circuit breaker (stop hammering a broken service), bulkhead (limit the damage), rate limiter (limit calls), fallback (return something useful).
/microservices/resilience/resilience4j.Circuit breaker states: Closed: calls go through. Open: calls fail immediately for a while. Half-open: a few test calls decide whether to close again.

/databases/relational-design.Normalisation: why and how far: Normalisation means each fact lives in one place. If a customer's name is stored on every order, changing it means many updates. Move it to a `customers` table and reference it by id. Three normal forms are enough for most designs.
/databases/relational-design.Keys: A primary key uniquely identifies a row. Prefer a meaningless id (sequence or UUID) over data that can change, like an email. A foreign key links a row in one table to the primary key of another.
/databases/relational-design.Constraints are your last line of defenc: Constraints make the database reject invalid data no matter which application writes it: `NOT NULL`, `UNIQUE`, `FOREIGN KEY`, `CHECK`. Application validation alone can be bypassed.
/databases/relational-design.Data types: Use `DECIMAL` for money (never float), store times in UTC, and use `BIGINT` for ids that may grow large.

/databases/sql-patterns.Joins: semantics matter: A join combines rows from two tables. INNER JOIN returns only rows that match in both. LEFT JOIN returns every row from the left table, with empty values where there is no match.
/databases/sql-patterns.Aggregation: GROUP BY, HAVING: `GROUP BY` collapses rows into groups so you can use `COUNT`, `SUM` and `AVG`. `WHERE` filters rows before grouping; `HAVING` filters the groups afterwards.
/databases/sql-patterns.Set-based work beats row-by-row: Let the database do bulk work with one statement (`UPDATE ... WHERE ...`) instead of looping in Java. One statement is far faster than thousands of round trips.
/databases/sql-patterns.Handling NULL: NULL means "unknown", so `NULL = NULL` is not true. Use `IS NULL`. Aggregates such as `AVG` ignore NULLs, and `COUNT(column)` skips them.

/databases/schema-migrations.Migrations as code: Put each schema change in a file such as `V2__add_status_index.sql`. The tool runs new files in order and records them. The database structure is now reviewed and versioned like code.
/databases/schema-migrations.Reference data and seed data: Reference data (countries, roles) that the app needs belongs in migrations. Test data does not: load it only in dev or test.

/databases/acid-isolation-mvcc.ACID: Atomic: all steps happen or none. Consistent: constraints always hold. Isolated: transactions do not see each other's half-done work. Durable: once committed, data survives a crash.

/messaging/kafka-fundamentals.Core concepts: A topic is a named stream of messages, split into partitions. Each message in a partition has an offset (its position). Order is guaranteed only inside one partition.
/messaging/kafka-fundamentals.Kafka vs traditional message queues: In a classic queue a message disappears once it is consumed. In Kafka messages stay for a retention period, so several independent consumers (and replays) are possible.

/messaging/kafka-consumers-offsets.Consumer groups: A consumer group shares a topic's work. Each partition is read by one consumer in the group. More consumers than partitions means some sit idle. A different group receives all the messages again.
/messaging/kafka-consumers-offsets.Offsets: An offset is a message's position in a partition. The consumer commits the offset to say "I have processed up to here", and resumes from there after a restart.

/messaging/rabbitmq-basics.The model: Producer, then exchange, then binding, then queue, then consumer. The exchange type (direct, fanout, topic) decides how messages are routed to queues.

/devops/docker-for-java.Layers and caching: Each Dockerfile step creates a layer, and Docker reuses unchanged layers. Copy rarely changing files (dependencies) before often-changing ones (your code) so rebuilds are quick.
/devops/docker-for-java.Docker Compose for local development: Compose starts your app plus its database or broker with one command, using a `compose.yaml` file. It is for local development and tests, not production.

/devops/kubernetes-basics.Architecture in one picture: A control plane (API server, scheduler, controllers) decides what should run; worker nodes run the containers. You talk only to the API server, usually with `kubectl`.
/devops/kubernetes-basics.Core objects: Pod: one or more containers. Deployment: keeps N pods running and does rolling updates. Service: a stable address with load balancing. ConfigMap and Secret: configuration. Ingress: HTTP entry from outside.

/devops/ci-cd.What a good pipeline does: A typical flow: commit, build and unit tests, static analysis and dependency scan, integration tests, build image, deploy to staging, smoke tests, production.
/devops/ci-cd.Test layers in CI: Run fast tests first: many unit tests, fewer integration tests with Testcontainers, a few end-to-end tests. Fast feedback keeps developers using the pipeline.

/devops/twelve-factor.I. *: One codebase in version control, many deployments (dev, staging, production). Not a separate fork per environment.
/devops/twelve-factor.II. *: Declare every dependency in the build file (`pom.xml`); never rely on something that just happens to be installed.
/devops/twelve-factor.III. *: Settings that differ per environment (URLs, passwords) come from environment variables or a config service, never from code.
/devops/twelve-factor.VII. *: The app serves HTTP itself by binding to a port (embedded Tomcat); it does not need an external web server.

/system-design/approach-and-estimation.A framework (about 45 minutes): Steps: 1) clarify requirements, 2) estimate numbers, 3) API and data model, 4) high-level design, 5) deep dives, 6) trade-offs and wrap-up. Say the plan out loud at the start.

/system-design/url-shortener.1. *: First decide what the system must do: create short links and redirect. Also agree what is out of scope (for example billing).
/system-design/url-shortener.2. *: Estimate: say 100 million new links a month is about 40 writes per second, and reads are 100 times higher, about 4,000 per second. Reads dominate, so caching matters.
/system-design/url-shortener.3. *: Define the API: `POST /urls` creates a short link and `GET /{code}` redirects to the original.
/system-design/url-shortener.4. *: The only real query is "find the URL by code", so a simple key-value table with the code as the primary key is enough.

/toolkit/coding-problems.Pattern cheat sheet: Match the problem to a pattern: pairs usually mean a hash map, a sorted array suggests two pointers, a contiguous range suggests a sliding window, brackets suggest a stack, top K suggests a heap.
/toolkit/coding-problems.1. *: Two Sum: store the numbers you have seen in a map; for each number check whether its partner is already in the map.
/toolkit/coding-problems.2. *: Valid Parentheses: use a stack; push each opening bracket and pop on each closing one, checking they match.
/toolkit/coding-problems.5. *: Group Anagrams: words with the same letters give the same key once sorted; group the words by that key in a map.
/toolkit/coding-problems.8. *: Linked lists: reversing means changing each `next` pointer; a cycle is detected with a slow and a fast pointer that eventually meet.
/toolkit/coding-problems.13. *: Min Stack: store the current minimum alongside every pushed value, so the minimum is always available in O(1).
/toolkit/coding-problems.16. *: These stream one-liners (grouping, averages, top words) are common warm-ups; know `groupingBy` and `toMap`.
/toolkit/coding-problems.How to practise: Practise by pattern, say your thinking aloud, and re-solve problems you missed after a week.
